messages.body_plain:
I'm considering have a table where each row describes an effect, and one
cell in the row is a density plot of the estimated distribution of the
effect.

ggplot seems oriented toward producing free-standing graphs; is this
something it could do?  How?

I think this differs from the usual output in two ways: the individual
graphs would be a small part of a page, and they might include only the
central plot area.

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

Like Doug, it's not clear to me what you really want. If you want to
produce densities at levels of a single factor or level combinations
of two factors, then faceting is what you probably want. OTOH, if you
want to place inset graphs at selected (spatial) locations, say on a
map, then you need a different type of solution. In a situation like
the latter case, it may be necessary to use the grid package directly,
generating the graphs as individual objects and positioning them
inside appropriately sized and positioned viewports. Your situation
sounds intermediate to the two scenarios outlined above, but without
some idea of the actual structure it's hard to recommend a single
course of action. I'll throw the ggsubplot package in as another
possibility, but I have no idea whether or not it would be helpful.

Dennis

I meant to send this suggestion to the whole list, but my phone
defaults to reply rather than reply-all.

What Keith is asking for is called a spark table, and they can be
produced using the sparkTable package. An introductory vignette can be
found at http://publik.tuwien.ac.at/files/PubDat_228663.pdf.

Here is a quick example similar to Keith's ASCII sketch:

library(reshape2)

mtcWide <- dcast(data.frame(car = rownames(mtcars),
                            mtcars[c("gear", "mpg")]),
                 ... ~ gear, value.var = "mpg")

names(mtcWide) <- paste("gears", names(mtcWide))

library(sparkTable)
summaryST(mtcWide[-1],
          outputType="html",
          filename = "mtcars",
          hist=TRUE,
          boxplot=FALSE,
          min=FALSE,
          quantile=FALSE,
          median=FALSE,
          mean=TRUE,
          max=FALSE)

Best,
Ista

I appreciate the idea of spark tables, but my limited interaction with
them was to compactly compare time series data in a dashboard. I don't
think they were meant to compare distributions in such a limited
space, but I could be wrong.

One way to get what you want in ggplot2 could be to facet by treatment
and to label the mean effect in each facet. By default, faceting
produces the same x- and y-limits. In the code below, I expand the
x-limits somewhat to provide enough room for the labels.

DF <- data.frame(trt = factor(rep(LETTERS[1:3], each = 100)),
                   y = rnorm(300, mean = rep(c(0.5, 0.1, -0.1), each = 100),
                                  sd = 0.1))

library(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

fx <- ddply(DF, "trt", summarise, y = round(mean(y), 2))
fx$lab <- paste0("Effect: ", fx$y)

# Treatments as facet labels, effects as annotation
ggplot(DF, aes(x = y)) +
   theme_bw() +
   geom_density(fill = "blue", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
   geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey30") +
   labs(x = "Effect", y = "Density") +
   xlim(-0.5, 1) +
   geom_text(data = fx, aes(x = -0.5, y = 4, label = lab), hjust = 0) +
   facet_wrap(~ trt, ncol = 1)

An alternative approach, although not particularly ideal, is to add
the treatments and effects as labels in each density plot. Here's how
it might work as a first draft on the above toy example, although with
more groups you want a more programmatic solution than this.

p1 <- ggplot(subset(DF, trt == "A"), aes(x = y)) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_density(fill = "blue", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey30") +
      labs(x = NULL, y = "") +
      xlim(-1.5, 1) +
      geom_text(x = -1.25, y = 4, label = "Treatment") +
      geom_text(x = -0.75, y = 4, label = "Effect") +
      geom_text(x = -1.25, y = 2, label = "A") +
      geom_text(x = -0.75, y = 2, label = fx[1, "y"]) +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

p2 <- ggplot(subset(DF, trt == "B"), aes(x = y)) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_density(fill = "blue", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey30") +
      labs(x = NULL, y = "") +
      xlim(-1.5, 1) +
      geom_text(x = -1.25, y = 2, label = "B") +
      geom_text(x = -0.75, y = 2, label = fx[2, "y"]) +
      theme(axis.text.x = element_blank())

p3 <- ggplot(subset(DF, trt == "C"), aes(x = y)) +
      theme_bw() +
      geom_density(fill = "blue", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
      geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey30") +
      labs(x = "Effect", y = "") +
      xlim(-1.5, 1) +
      geom_text(x = -1.25, y = 2, label = "C") +
      geom_text(x = -0.75, y = 2, label = fx[3, "y"])

library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 1)

A third approach would be to create a gridTable of the appropriate
size for the treatments and effect along with the initial ggplot (sans
the annotation), each saved to an object. You might then do something
like

grid.arrange(my_grid_table, my_faceted_ggplot, nrow = 1)

with appropriate sizing in the x-direction, to generate a side-by-side
table with corresponding densities. See ?grid.arrange for further
details.

If any of these options appeal to you (and they may not), you'll still
need to fiddle with the size and type of graphic to export to your
Word document. This example is simply to illustrate different
possibilities with ggplot2. Your real example may contain far more
levels, enough so to make these illustrations impractical for your use
case. In my example, I also took the label positions from a
preliminary view of the graph; if you want a more programmatic
solution, you'll have to DIY.

Dennis

You can certainly construct the graphs and insert them into a table
yourself, perhaps something along the lines of

d_ply(mtcars, "gear",
      function(x) {
          p <-ggplot(x, aes(x = mpg)) +
                  geom_density(fill = "grey60") +
                  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(.025, 0)) +
                  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(.025, 0)) +
                          theme_minimal()
          gt <- ggplot_gtable(ggplot_build(p))
          ge <- subset(gt$layout, name == "panel")
          png(paste(unique(x$gear), "png", sep="."),
              width = 80,
              height = 60)
          grid.draw(gt[ge$t:ge$b, ge$l:ge$r])
          dev.off()
      }
      )

The simplest way to do this in ggplot2 is to follow Tom's advice about faceting by year:

# The way you should have presented your data, output from the dput() function
DF <- structure(list(year = c(2005L, 2005L, 2005L, 2005L, 2005L, 2005L,
2006L, 2006L, 2006L, 2006L, 2006L, 2006L), factor1 = structure(c(1L,
1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("A",
"B"), class = "factor"), factor2 = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L,
2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("1", "2", "3"), class = "factor"),
    value = c(4L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L)), .Names = c("year",
"factor1", "factor2", "value"), row.names = c(NA, -12L), class = "data.frame")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(DF, aes(x = factor1, y = value, fill = factor2)) +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_histogram(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
    facet_wrap(~ year) +
    theme(panel.margin = grid::unit(0, "lines"))

Why was it necessary to point out dput()? This was the output when I copied and pasted the data from your e-mail into R using read.table():

# read.table(header = TRUE, sep = "\t", text = "
# <your data copied/pasted here>
# ")

   yearfactor1factor2value
1                  2005A14

4                  2005B12
5                  2005B22
6                  2005B33

This is why you don't copy and paste data into an e-mail that goes to a text-based list. The correct way to do it is to call dput() on your data object and paste its output into your e-mail, as I did above. For example, I kept your object in a data frame DF, so to get a text representation of the object, type

dput(DF)

which returns the part above starting with structure(.   It took me six tries of space insertions to finally get your data read in; it should not have been necessary to do that.

To get the histogram as shown in your Excel graph requires a bit more work. Here's one attempt: it requires removing the legend in the left plot, the y-axis information in the right plot and then making some adjustments in plot margins to more or less equalize the widths of the bars.It isn't an aesthetic masterpiece, but it's an OK first draft.

p1 <- ggplot(subset(DF, year = 2005),
             aes(x = factor1, y = value, fill = factor2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        geom_histogram(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
        xlab("2005") + scale_fill_hue(guide = "none") +
        theme(plot.margin = unit(c(1, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5), "lines"))

p2 <- ggplot(subset(DF, year = 2006),
             aes(x = factor1, y = value, fill = factor2)) +
        theme_bw() +
        geom_histogram(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +
        labs(x = "2006", y = NULL) +
        theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(),
              axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
              legend.position = c(0.85, 0.9),
              legend.text = element_text(size = rel(1)),
              legend.title = element_text(size = rel(1.2)),
              plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1.5, 0.5, 1.5), "lines"))

# library(gridExtra)
grid.arrange(p1, p2, nrow = 1)

I put the legend inside the second plot to avoid having to mess around too much with plot margins and to avoid having to use the gtable package to grab the legend and position it on the graphics page. There are a few posts floating around, mostly on StackOverflow, showing how to do such things if you're determined to have a legend on the right, but I'll let you chase that if you're inclined to do so.

Dennis

In facet_wrap(), you'd add the argument nrow = 1. You'd probably want to control the aspect ratio of the result, though, since the default panels will be thin and tall. Here's one approach:

# Thank you for supplying data with dput()  :)
DF <- structure(list(year = structure(c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L,

2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 3L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L, 4L,
4L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 5L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 6L, 7L, 7L, 7L,
7L, 7L, 7L), .Label = c("2005", "2006", "2007", "2008", "2009",
"2010", "2011"), class = "factor"), factor1 = structure(c(1L,
1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L,
2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L,
2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 2L, 2L, 2L), .Label = c("A", "B"), class = "factor"),
    factor2 = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L,
    1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L,
    1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L,
    1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("1", "2", "3"), class = "factor"),
    value = c(4L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L,
    5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L,
    2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L, 5L, 3L, 3L, 2L, 2L, 3L
    )), .Names = c("year", "factor1", "factor2", "value"), row.names = c(NA,
-42L), class = "data.frame")

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = factor1, y = value, fill = factor2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_histogram(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +

  facet_wrap(~ year, nrow = 1) +
  theme(panel.margin = grid::unit(0, "lines"),
        aspect.ratio = 2)

# compared to

ggplot(DF, aes(x = factor1, y = value, fill = factor2)) +
  theme_bw() +
  geom_histogram(stat = "identity", position = "stack") +

  facet_wrap(~ year, nrow = 1) +

  theme(panel.margin = grid::unit(0, "lines"))

If the modification is OK and you want to put it in a report, it's probably best to save it with ggsave() and specify height and width arguments so that you can control the amount of white space above and below the graph. See ?ggsave for details.

Dennis

Hi Zongtai, sorry for the slow response--been traveling. To separate years, one option would be to use facets; another is to have dummy data that separate the years and are displayed with blank tick labels. For example:

# Create label information and add dummy data
DF$label <- paste(DF[[1]],DF[[2]] , sep="\n")
DF <- rbind(DF,data.frame(year=2005:2011,factor1="C",value=0,factor2=1,label=""))

# We want one label per year & factor1 combination, ordered correctly
labeldata <- subset(DF,factor2==1)
labeldata <- labeldata[order(labeldata$year,labeldata$factor1),]

# Plot
ggplot(DF,aes(paste0(year,"\n",factor1),value))+geom_bar(aes(fill=factor2),position="stack",stat="identity")+scale_x_discrete(labels=labeldata$label)

Dennis or others may have better ideas here.

Ben

  X v time (A)   ||   X v time (B)
  Y v time (A)   ||   Y v time (B)

Thanks in advance for you any guidance you can provide!

Cheers,
David Romano

Hi:

I'm not exactly sure that I interpreted your request correctly, but
here's one shot at it.

# Read in the data
test.df <- structure(list(ID = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), group =
structure(c(1L,
2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("A", "B", "C"), class = "factor"),
    X = c(-0.2300575, -0.8592283, 0.5961568, 0.4895552, 1.8303039,
    0.6726456), Y = c(0.59433108, -0.04834775, 0.13914823, -0.10457984,
    -0.06716994, -1.58981685), Z = c(0.7463163, -0.3927258, 0.6158333,
    -1.2070888, 0.1888753, 1.7563034), time = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L,
    2L, 2L)), .Names = c("ID", "group", "X", "Y", "Z", "time"
), class = "data.frame", row.names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5",
"6"))

library(ggplot2)

# Plot X and Y separately over time by group
ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = X,
color = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) + xlab("time")

ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = Y,
color = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) + labs(x = "time")

# Add lines to the plot
ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = X,
color = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_line(aes(group = group), size = 1) + xlab("time")

ggplot(subset(test.df, group != "C"), aes(x = factor(time), y = Y,
color = group)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_line(aes(group = group), size = 1) + xlab("time")

A few comments:

1. It worked this time, but it is usually a bad idea to copy and paste
data from the R console into an e-mail. It's better to call the dput()
function and copy/paste the output from that:

> dput(test.df)
structure(list(ID = c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), group = structure(c(1L,
2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), .Label = c("A", "B", "C"), class = "factor"),
    X = c(-0.2300575, -0.8592283, 0.5961568, 0.4895552, 1.8303039,
    0.6726456), Y = c(0.59433108, -0.04834775, 0.13914823, -0.10457984,
    -0.06716994, -1.58981685), Z = c(0.7463163, -0.3927258, 0.6158333,
    -1.2070888, 0.1888753, 1.7563034), time = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 2L,
    2L, 2L)), .Names = c("ID", "group", "X", "Y", "Z", "time"
), class = "data.frame", row.names = c("1", "2", "3", "4", "5",
"6"))

dput() outputs a textual representation of the structure of an R
object. It guarantees that anyone who pops it into her R session will
see the same object you do. Moreover, it avoids formatting issues when
copying from another application such as Excel or Word. Why is dput()
good? Because anyone can copy/paste the above version of test.df into
an R session and see the same structure I sent:

> str(test.df)
'data.frame':   6 obs. of  6 variables:
 $ ID   : int  1 2 3 1 2 3
 $ group: Factor w/ 3 levels "A","B","C": 1 2 3 1 2 3
 $ X    : num  -0.23 -0.859 0.596 0.49 1.83 ...
 $ Y    : num  0.5943 -0.0483 0.1391 -0.1046 -0.0672 ...
 $ Z    : num  0.746 -0.393 0.616 -1.207 0.189 ...
 $ time : int  1 1 1 2 2 2

If the data object is large, one can put it in Dropbox or some on-line
data repository that people can download from an URL into R (not
necessarily in dput form, but one that R can input easily).

2. More specific to the plots above, when the x-variable is a factor,
geom_line() or geom_path() won't render unless you have mapped a group
aesthetic. Notice that one can map aesthetics within a geom call, in
which case the mapping is local to the geom. When aesthetics are
mapped in ggplot(), it is assumed that they are 'global' - i.e., to be
available in _every_ subsequent geom/stat call. This is one of the
first lessons that a new user of ggplot2 needs to know - the
distinction between setting an aesthetic to a constant value or
mapping it to a variable. Mappings always take place within aes();
setting of aesthetics always takes place outside of aes(). For
example, in geom_point(), the point size was set to 3 and in
geom_line, the size (line thickness) was set to 1.

I hope this is a correct interpretation of your question.

Dennis

library(ggplot2)

                        values=c("solid", "dashed"),

  theme(strip.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
        strip.text.x = element_text(size = rel(1.4))) +
  facet_wrap(~ area, ncol = 3)

To modify non-data aspects of a ggplot, such as the appearance of the
facet strips, use the theming system. You can see the elements and the
default values of their properties by typing 'theme_grey' at the
prompt (without the quotes). In this case, the specification 'size =
rel(1.4)'  in strip.text.x increases the default strip text size by
40%.

The values argument of a scale function refers to the values of the
aesthetic to be plotted in the graphic, while the labels argument
refers to the labels to be placed in the legend. Implicitly, the
breaks argument refers to the levels of the factor mapped to the
aesthetic, which in this case are 'boxcox' and 'fcast'. Therefore,
level 'boxcox' is associated with a solid line and legend label
'Box-Cox', whereas level 'fcast' is associated with a dashed line and
legend label 'e'.

messages.subject_clean: Tweaking ggplot2 plots, faster redraw or WSIWYG-style editing?
messages.body_plain:
Often ggplot2 will immediately produce almost the plot that I want and only after much effort am I able to get a finished product.

I often have a ggplot2 command at the end of a fairly expensive R script. The script accesses a large amount of data and rearranges the data inside the script but doesn't produce any new data. Simply drawing the plot from the ggplot command takes more than I want to wait if I'm making small tweaks.

If I'm unlikely to produce the plot again with different data I simply resort to Illustrator. For plots I'll produce again, I usually settle for what I have even though the changes that I'd like to make are very easy to express to another human.

My question in general is, what is a reasonably efficient workflow for getting a plot "just-so"?

Is there any way to edit a ggplot2 plot interactively and then produce an R command that would have produced that plot?

Alternatively, is there a way to quickly redraw a ggplot2 output if I'm only making small changes to the R command that produces the plot?

Thanks.

messages.subject_clean: Tweaking ggplot2 plots, faster redraw or WSIWYG-style editing?
messages.body_plain:
I don't know of any GUI/WYSIWYG editing, but I also run into the same issues when I work with large data. The key for my work flow is that I sample the data, using `sample` to render quickly and then add all of the features I want, like coloring, faceting, labels, etc., before using the full data set. Sometimes the sampling needs to be a bit more complex to make sure I get all values of discrete variable, but that takes much less time to do than watching a plot render with the full data.

Also, I make strong use of the `+` operator as I add components. So I basically will do something like `p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)` and then play with it like, `p + ylab("Foo")` or `p + ylab("Bar")` to figure out what I want before committing the final plot, which would just be `p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y) + ylab("Foo")`. Once I have settled on everything, I kick off the "full" plotting and work on something else while in renders. I also use the `beepr` package's `beep` to give me an audio cue when it is done.

I'm not sure what I do is a great process, so I curious to hear from others.

Cheers,
Doug

messages.body_plain:
Problem 1: No reproducible example.
Problem 2: You allude to the function multiplot(). Assuming it comes
from an R package and is not one of your own invention, there are at
least six CRAN packages with a function named multiplot(): coefplot,
blowtorch, phonTools, abf2, optiRum and Rmisc, which i got from

library(sos)
findFn("multiplot")

You have not mentioned where your multiplot() function comes from.

David Guy has pointed out a simple solution to your problem:

library(gridExtra)
do.call(grid.arrange, obj)

Note that ggplots are produced from grid graphics, so if you're using
a multiplot() function from somewhere, you should make sure that it
supports grid graphics objects. The gridExtra package does; I have no
idea about the others.

To answer your last question, it is highly unlikely that unequal
numbers of bars are the problem since the plots are saved in separate
objects. Below is a reproducible example.

# Create four data frames - note the unequal number of categories
ds1 <- data.frame(x = sample(LETTERS[1:5], 100, replace = TRUE))
ds2 <- data.frame(x = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 100, replace = TRUE))
ds3 <- data.frame(x = sample(LETTERS[1:6], 100, replace = TRUE))
ds4 <- data.frame(x = sample(LETTERS[1:5], 100, replace = TRUE))

# Create a simple function to plot a single data frame
plotfun <- function(d)
{
    require(ggplot2)
    ggplot(d, aes(x = x)) + geom_bar(fill = "darkorange")
}

# Create a list of ggplot objects
L <- lapply(paste0("ds", 1:4), function(z) plotfun(get(z)))

# Use do.call() to invoke grid.arrange() on the list of plots
library(gridExtra)
do.call(grid.arrange, L)

## Another way that avoids do.call() and allows
# grid.arrange() arguments to be specified - plot
# objects are in the global environment rather than a list object

p1 <- ggplot(ds1, aes(x = x)) + geom_bar(fill = "darkorange")
p2 <- p1 %+% ds2    # Same plot structure as p1, using data ds2
p3 <- p1 %+% ds3
p4 <- p1 %+% ds4

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)

Dennis

Hi everyone,

I'm new to ggplot and need some help with bar graphs. Online different solutions were offered but none seemed to work for me (perhaps because they were for older versions?).

I would like N bar charts next to each other one for the each subpopulation (i.e. N =2 so a bar chart for A=0 and one for A=1). In each bar chart I want to graph the categorical variable B (say B=0, B=1) on the x-axis and the percentage of the subpopulation's total C on the y-axis.
In particular the percentages in each subgroup add up to 100% (i.e. for A=0, B=0 has 25% of the C and B=1 has 75% of the C).

The data looks like this
A  B C
0  0  75
0  1  12
0  1  12
0  1   1
1  0  33
1  1  34
1  0  33

So here I want a bar chart for group A which shows that for A=0, 75% of the total C of A=0 falls into B=0, and 25% of it fall into B=1. For A=1 we have 66% falling into B=0 and 34% falling into B=1.

Please let me know if you'd need more information to understand my problem.
Thank you very much for your help,

Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: scale_fill_brewer() - specify na.colour and include NA in legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I would like to use scale_fill_brewer and the option to colour NAs by a specific colour, but include NAs in the legend. Reproducible example below.  Couple of options I've tried are commented out. I know if you aren't using scale_fill_brewer there's a work around by changing NA to something else in the data (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/18970580/how-to-plot-na-bar-with-ggplot2), but that would defeat me trying to use a sequential scale from brewer along with a very different colour for NA.  The legend item doesn't need to be called "NA".

I've gone from integer to a factor in the example because that's what I do with my real data (I'm leaving justifications for doing what is pretty much a stacked histogram out as the principle applies more widely anyhow).

Any thoughts?
Best wishes,
Olivia

#install.packages("vegan")
#install.packages("ggplot2")
require(vegan)
require(ggplot2)

data(mite.env) # dataset from mite
miteenv_na <- mite.env # not to pollute mite if already using it
miteenv_na$familiarity <- sample(1:5)
miteenv_na[ , 6][sample(seq(miteenv_na[ , 6]), 10)] <- NA #introducing NAs
is.na <http://is.na>(miteenv_na[ , 6]) # checking
miteenv_na$familiarity_fac <- factor(miteenv_na$familiarity, exclude = NULL)
levels(miteenv_na$familiarity_fac)
fam_labs <- levels(miteenv_na$familiarity_fac)

ggplot(miteenv_na, aes(x = Topo))+
  geom_bar(position = position_fill(),
           stat = "bin",
           aes(fill = familiarity_fac)) +
  scale_fill_brewer("Familiarity",
                    type = "seq",
                    na.value = "orange",
                    #labels = levels(miteenv_na$familiarity_fac))+ #doesn't work
                    #labels = fam_labs) + #also doesn't work
  labs(y = "proportion") +
  theme_bw()
